Jeremiah 27.audience: Early in Zedekiah's reign, envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon come to Jerusalem, apparently to plan revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah wears a yoke and tells them to submit (Jeremiah 27:2–3).

culture.title: Bonds and yokes
culture.text: A wooden yoke with leather straps bound oxen together for plowing—a picture of subjection to a foreign king.

culture.title: Temple vessels in Babylon
culture.text: Babylon carried temple vessels away in 597 BC. False prophets promised their quick return; Cyrus returned them about sixty years later (Ezra 1:7–11).

Jeremiah 28.audience: In the fourth year of Zedekiah, the prophet Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke and promises the exiles will return within two years. Hananiah dies that same year (Jeremiah 28:17).

culture.title: Yokes of wood and iron
culture.text: Breaking a wooden yoke only leads to an iron one—a harder subjection.

culture.title: Testing prophets
culture.text: A prophet of peace would be known as true only when his word came to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Jeremiah 29.audience: Jeremiah writes a letter to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and "seek the peace of the city" (Jeremiah 29:7).

culture.title: Letters carried by envoys
culture.text: The letter travels with Zedekiah's envoys to Nebuchadnezzar. Official messengers often carried private letters too.

culture.title: Exiles in Babylon
culture.text: Babylonian records show Jewish exiles living in their own communities, such as ‘the town of Judah’ (Al-Yahudu), farming and doing business.

culture.title: Roasted in the fire
culture.text: Nebuchadnezzar executed two false prophets by burning; Daniel 3 also describes a furnace punishment.

Jeremiah 30.audience: Jeremiah 30–33 is often called the Book of Consolation. God tells Jeremiah to write these words in a book (Jeremiah 30:2) for a future return.

culture.title: A woman in labor
culture.text: Men holding their sides like women in childbirth picture terror and pain.

culture.title: Breaking the yoke
culture.text: God promises to break the yoke from Israel's neck and burst their bonds.

Jeremiah 31.audience: Jeremiah promises a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34), quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8–12. Matthew quotes verse 15 of Herod's massacre in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:17–18).

culture.title: Rachel weeping in Ramah
culture.text: Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, was buried near Bethlehem. Ramah, north of Jerusalem, was where exiles were gathered for deportation (Jeremiah 40:1).

culture.title: Sour grapes
culture.text: A proverb said children suffered for their fathers' sins. Ezekiel quotes the same proverb (Ezekiel 18:2).

culture.title: Measuring the city
culture.text: The rebuilt city's boundaries are named: the tower of Hananeel, the corner gate, the hill Gareb, and the brook Kidron.

Jeremiah 32.audience: In the tenth year of Zedekiah, during the siege, Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth from his cousin as a sign that land will be bought again in Judah (Jeremiah 32:1, 15).

culture.title: A deed of purchase
culture.text: Jeremiah signs, seals, and witnesses the deed and weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. Legal documents were written twice—one copy sealed, one open.

culture.title: Kept in an earthen vessel
culture.text: Documents were stored in clay jars to last a long time; the Dead Sea Scrolls were preserved the same way.

culture.title: Redemption right
culture.text: As next of kin, Jeremiah had the right and duty to redeem family land (Leviticus 25:25).

Jeremiah 33.audience: While still in prison, Jeremiah hears promises of restored houses, fields, and the line of David and the Levitical priests (Jeremiah 33:1, 17–18).

culture.title: Houses torn down for siege works
culture.text: Houses were pulled down to strengthen the walls against siege mounds.

culture.title: Flocks counted again
culture.text: Shepherds counted their sheep as they passed under the hand—a sign of peaceful life restored.

Jeremiah 34.audience: When only Lachish and Azekah remained of Judah's fortified cities (Jeremiah 34:7), Zedekiah and the people freed their Hebrew slaves—then took them back.

culture.title: The Lachish letters
culture.text: Ostraca found at Lachish include a message saying the writer could no longer see the signals of Azekah—from the same final days.

culture.title: Passing between the calf
culture.text: The covenant was made by cutting a calf in two and walking between the pieces, as in Genesis 15:9–17.

culture.title: Releasing Hebrew slaves
culture.text: The law required Hebrew servants to be freed after six years (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12).

Jeremiah 35.audience: In Jehoiakim's days, Jeremiah offers wine to the Rechabites, who refuse because of their ancestor Jonadab's command (Jeremiah 35:6).

culture.title: The Rechabites
culture.text: The Rechabites lived in tents, drank no wine, and built no houses or vineyards. Jonadab son of Rechab had joined Jehu (2 Kings 10:15).

culture.title: Chambers of the temple
culture.text: The temple had side chambers used by priests, prophets, and officials.

Jeremiah 36.audience: In the fourth and fifth years of Jehoiakim, Baruch writes Jeremiah's words on a scroll and reads them in the temple. The king burns it, and Jeremiah dictates it again with more added (Jeremiah 36:32).

culture.title: A winter house and a brazier
culture.text: In the ninth month (December), the king sat in his winter house by a fire burning in a brazier.

culture.title: A penknife
culture.text: A scribe's knife was used to trim reed pens and cut scrolls. The king cuts off columns as they are read and throws them in the fire.

culture.title: Gemariah son of Shaphan
culture.text: A clay seal impression reading ‘Gemaryahu son of Shaphan’ was found in the City of David.

Jeremiah 37.audience: During a pause in the siege, when Babylon withdrew to meet an Egyptian army, Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:11–15).

culture.title: An Egyptian relief force
culture.text: Pharaoh's army marched out, and the Babylonians lifted the siege briefly to face it.

culture.title: Bread from the bakers' street
culture.text: Jeremiah receives a daily loaf "out of the bakers' street"—trades were grouped in particular streets.

Jeremiah 38.audience: Princes lower Jeremiah into a muddy cistern, and Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian official, rescues him (Jeremiah 38:6–13).

culture.title: A dungeon cistern
culture.text: Cisterns cut in rock held rainwater; when dry they had mud at the bottom and were used as prisons.

culture.title: Old rags under the armholes
culture.text: Ebedmelech gives Jeremiah old clothes to pad the ropes as he is pulled up.

culture.title: Jehucal and Gedaliah
culture.text: Seal impressions naming ‘Jehucal son of Shelemiah’ and ‘Gedaliah son of Pashur’ have been found in Jerusalem.

Jeremiah 39.audience: Jerusalem falls in the eleventh year of Zedekiah (586 BC) (Jeremiah 39:2). Readers would see Babylon's officers take their seats in the middle gate.

culture.title: Babylonian officials
culture.text: Nergalsharezer and Sarsechim are named. A Babylonian tablet names an official Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, possibly Sarsechim.

culture.title: Blinding a rebel king
culture.text: Zedekiah's eyes are put out and he is chained—the penalty for breaking an oath to the overlord.

Jeremiah 40.audience: Jeremiah is released at Ramah and chooses to stay in the land with Gedaliah, whom Babylon appointed governor at Mizpah (Jeremiah 40:5–6).

culture.title: A governor at Mizpah
culture.text: Babylon appointed a local governor over those left in the land. A seal reading ‘belonging to Gedaliah who is over the house’ was found at Lachish.

culture.title: Gathering summer fruit
culture.text: The remnant gathered wine and summer fruits "very much"—the land kept producing after the fall.

Jeremiah 41.audience: Ishmael, of the royal family, murders Gedaliah at Mizpah in the seventh month (Jeremiah 41:1–2). Jews later kept a fast in the seventh month to remember it (Zechariah 7:5).

culture.title: Mourners from the north
culture.text: Eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria come with shaven beards and torn clothes, bringing offerings to the ruined temple.

culture.title: A cistern from Asa's day
culture.text: Ishmael throws the bodies into the large cistern King Asa made when fortifying Mizpah (1 Kings 15:22).

Jeremiah 42.audience: The survivors ask Jeremiah to pray for guidance and promise to obey. After ten days the answer comes: stay in the land and do not go to Egypt.

culture.title: Seeking an oracle
culture.text: Jeremiah waits ten days for the word of the LORD—prophets did not always receive answers at once.

Jeremiah 43.audience: The leaders take the remnant, Jeremiah, and Baruch to Egypt, to Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:5–7), a border fortress in the eastern Delta.

culture.title: Stones in the brick pavement
culture.text: Jeremiah buries large stones in the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh's house at Tahpanhes as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne there.

culture.title: Bethshemesh in Egypt
culture.text: Bethshemesh, ‘house of the sun,’ is Heliopolis (On), famous for its obelisks ("images").

Jeremiah 44.audience: Jeremiah speaks to Jews living in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph (Memphis), and Pathros in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1). They insist on burning incense to the queen of heaven.

culture.title: Jewish communities in Egypt
culture.text: Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, on the Nile in southern Egypt, show a Jewish military colony there in the fifth century BC with its own temple.

culture.title: Cakes for the queen of heaven
culture.text: The women made cakes bearing her image and poured out drink offerings, with their husbands' approval.

Jeremiah 45.audience: A short message to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when he wrote the scroll.

culture.title: Baruch the scribe
culture.text: Professional scribes wrote documents for others. A clay seal impression reading ‘Berekyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe’ has been published, though its origin is debated.

Jeremiah 46.audience: Jeremiah 46–51 contains oracles against the nations. Chapter 46 concerns Egypt and the battle of Carchemish in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605 BC).

culture.title: Carchemish
culture.text: At Carchemish on the Euphrates, Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho, ending Egyptian power in Syria. The Babylonian Chronicle records the battle.

culture.title: Balm for Egypt
culture.text: "Go up into Gilead, and take balm"—Egypt's medicines will not heal its wound.

Jeremiah 47.audience: An oracle against the Philistines, "before that Pharaoh smote Gaza" (Jeremiah 47:1).

culture.title: The rumbling of chariot wheels
culture.text: Fathers flee without turning back for their children at the noise of horses' hoofs and chariots.

culture.title: Caphtor
culture.text: The Philistines are "the remnant of the country of Caphtor," usually identified with Crete (Amos 9:7).

Jeremiah 48.audience: A long oracle against Moab, naming its towns—Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Dibon, Aroer, Kerioth—and its god Chemosh (Jeremiah 48:7).

culture.title: Wine settled on its lees
culture.text: Wine left on its sediment (lees) without being poured off kept its flavor but grew thick—Moab undisturbed and complacent.

culture.title: Chemosh
culture.text: Chemosh was Moab's national god, named on the Moabite Stone.

Jeremiah 49.audience: Oracles against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam. Obadiah 1:1–6 closely parallels Jeremiah 49:9–16 about Edom.

culture.title: Rabbah of the Ammonites
culture.text: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, is modern Amman, Jordan.

culture.title: Teman's wisdom
culture.text: Edom's Teman was famous for wise men; Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite (Job 2:11).

culture.title: Elam
culture.text: Elam lay east of Babylon in what is now southwestern Iran; its archers were famous (Isaiah 22:6).

Jeremiah 50.audience: A long oracle against Babylon, the power that destroyed Jerusalem. It calls Israel to flee from Babylon as from the Chaldeans' land (Jeremiah 50:8).

culture.title: Bel and Merodach
culture.text: Merodach (Marduk), also called Bel, was Babylon's chief god.

culture.title: A nation from the north
culture.text: The Medes and Persians who conquered Babylon in 539 BC came from the north and east.

culture.title: Drought on her waters
culture.text: Babylon depended on the Euphrates and a network of canals.

Jeremiah 51.audience: The oracle against Babylon continues. Jeremiah sends it with Seraiah, who goes to Babylon with Zedekiah, to read and then sink in the Euphrates (Jeremiah 51:59–64).

culture.title: A golden cup
culture.text: Babylon is "a golden cup in the LORD's hand, that made all the earth drunken." Revelation uses the image (Revelation 17:4).

culture.title: Babylon's walls
culture.text: Babylon's broad walls and high gates were famous; Herodotus describes walls wide enough for a chariot to turn on top.

culture.title: A scroll sunk in the river
culture.text: Seraiah ties a stone to the scroll and throws it into the Euphrates as a sign of Babylon's fall.

Jeremiah 52.audience: The final chapter repeats the account of Jerusalem's fall from 2 Kings 24:18–25:30 and adds numbers of those deported (Jeremiah 52:28–30).

culture.title: Three deportations
culture.text: Jeremiah lists 3,023 deported in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 832 in his eighteenth, and 745 in his twenty-third—4,600 persons in all.

culture.title: Temple bronze
culture.text: The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, stands, and sea and carried off the metal.

culture.title: Jehoiachin's release
culture.text: Evilmerodach (Amel-Marduk) released Jehoiachin. Babylonian ration tablets list oil for ‘Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud.’

Lamentations 1.audience: Lamentations was written after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. Jewish tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, and it is read in synagogues on the fast of the ninth of Av, which mourns the temple's destruction.

culture.title: An acrostic
culture.text: Chapter 1 has twenty-two verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

culture.title: Jerusalem as a widow
culture.text: "How is she become as a widow!" Widows had lost protection and status. The city sits alone weeping.

culture.title: Tribute city
culture.text: "She that was great among the nations... how is she become tributary!"

Lamentations 2.audience: The second poem describes God's anger against Jerusalem—its walls, palaces, temple, priests, and children.

culture.title: Dust on the head
culture.text: The elders sit on the ground in silence, throw dust on their heads, and wear sackcloth—the customs of deep mourning.

culture.title: Hissing and wagging heads
culture.text: Passers-by clap their hands, hiss, and wag their heads—gestures of scorn.

culture.title: Children fainting in the streets
culture.text: During the siege famine, children faint and die in the streets asking for bread and wine.

Lamentations 3.audience: The third poem has sixty-six verses, three for each Hebrew letter. In the middle it says, "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:22–23).

culture.title: Walled in
culture.text: "He hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out"—like a prisoner or a besieged city.

culture.title: Gravel stones in the mouth
culture.text: Bread baked in ashes could be full of grit—an image of bitter suffering.

culture.title: A man and his yoke
culture.text: "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth"—the yoke as a picture of discipline.

Lamentations 4.audience: The fourth poem contrasts Jerusalem before and after the siege, including its princes, priests, and king.

culture.title: Gold become dim
culture.text: Gold dulled and holy stones scattered in the streets picture the temple's treasures and Zion's people cast down.

culture.title: Nazarites blackened
culture.text: Those who had been purer than snow and healthier than milk become blacker than coal with hunger.

culture.title: Rejoice, O Edom
culture.text: Edom, "that dwellest in the land of Uz," gloated at Jerusalem's fall (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 1:11–14).

Lamentations 5.audience: The final poem is a communal prayer with twenty-two verses but not an acrostic. It ends asking God to turn his people back to him.

culture.title: Paying for water and wood
culture.text: "We have drunken our water for money; our wood is sold unto us"—the survivors must buy what was once their own.

culture.title: Grinding and carrying wood
culture.text: Young men are made to grind at the mill, the work of slaves, and boys stagger under loads of wood.

culture.title: Foxes on Zion
culture.text: Jackals (foxes) walk on the ruined temple mount—a sign of total desolation.
